clue.text: Exaggerate to impress as 11 might, supplied with 19?

definitions.meaning: the idiom: overdo praise or emphasis

definitions.text: to impress as 11 might, supplied with 19
definitions.meaning: a BRICKLAYER (11) spreads MORTAR (19) with a flat-bladed hand tool, pressing it on literally

explanation.surface: Advice on how to make an impression, borrowing a tradesman and his materials from elsewhere in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references are the joke: 11 is BRICKLAYER and 19 is MORTAR, so the second half describes the idiom done literally on a building site.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for overdoing praise, pictured as slapping on far more than is needed, as a builder slaps on mortar.

clue.text: Catholic washing in loo, adult with sweaty smell

parts.note: LAV is short for lavatory
A = adult, the film certificate
BO = body odour

explanation.surface: An unpleasant trip to a public toilet where someone is cleaning up amid a sweaty stink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catholic washing' is not a description of the loo scene but the definition: the priest's ritual rinsing of hands at Mass.
explanation.definitionFit: The lavabo is the ritual washing of the celebrant's hands in the Catholic Mass.

clue.text: Criminal excitedly ready when taking in island

indicators.note: READY is stirred up into a new order
the anagram takes the island letter inside it

parts.note: READY rearranged
I = island, the map abbreviation

explanation.surface: A crook getting keyed up and prepared as he lands on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The island's I sits between YARD and E of the rearranged READY.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yardie is a member of a Jamaican criminal gang.

clue.text: Show foresight: take hand to shake without greeting?

indicators.note: TAKE HAND is shaken into a new order
the jumbled letters sit outside the greeting

parts.note: TAKE HAND rearranged
HI is a greeting

explanation.surface: A handshake offered without a hello, with a note about anticipating things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside: HI goes after the first T of the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To think ahead is to plan for what is coming, showing foresight.

clue.text: Operatic heroine wants no cat skinned outside room

indicators.note: NO and A go around the room letters
CAT loses its skin, the outer letters C and T

parts.note: as written
RM is the abbreviation for room
cAt with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A diva making demands: no cat in the dressing room.
explanation.walkthrough: Norma is the title heroine of Bellini's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma, the druid priestess, is the heroine of Bellini's opera of that name.

clue.text: Black cat runs for ball pitched short

parts.note: B = black, as on pencils
the ounce is the snow leopard
R = runs, the cricket scorebook abbreviation

explanation.surface: A black cat running on to the pitch during a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cat' is the wild kind: OUNCE, another name for the snow leopard. In cricket a bouncer is a short-pitched delivery that rears up at the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouncer is a ball pitched short so that it bounces up high at the batter.

clue.text: Novelist's written about energy company partner

indicators.note: the novelist's name is set down around the company

parts.note: Saul Bellow, the American novelist; the 's is 'is'
EDF, the French-owned energy company that supplies British homes

explanation.surface: A literary author has published a book about a power firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novelist's' reads as possessive but the 's is 'is': the novelist is written around the company.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedfellow is an associate or partner, as in strange bedfellows.

clue.text: Fruit munter picked up

indicators.note: what is picked up by the ear is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a munter is British slang for an ugly person

explanation.surface: An unattractive person gathering fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Munter is British slang for an unattractive person, so it gives UGLY. The ugli is a knobbly Jamaican citrus fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a citrus fruit, a cross of grapefruit and tangerine.

clue.text: Rising power to do penance in church and sepulchral monument

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising turns the letters to read upwards

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
P = power, as in physics
to atone is to make amends

explanation.surface: A penitent in church beside a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' only makes sense in a down entry, where the power-and-penance letters are read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: A cenotaph is a monument to the dead, in the style of a tomb but empty.

clue.text: Snakes — excellent specimens!

definitions.meaning: a rattler is informal for a first-rate example of something, as in a rattling good yarn

explanation.surface: An admiring remark on a collection of fine snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is dated slang: a rattler is a cracking good one of its kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattlers are rattlesnakes, and in old slang also excellent examples of anything.

clue.text: Decision avoiding court for Italian musician

indicators.note: the word steers clear of the court letters, dropping them

parts.note: a verdict is a jury's decision
CT is the abbreviation for court; removed

explanation.surface: An Italian composer settling a matter out of court.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CT from VERDICT and the composer of Aida is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the great Italian opera composer.

clue.text: Large body Jellicoe ultimately found among poinsettia?

indicators.note: take the last letter of Jellicoe

parts.note: the poinsettia, with its scarlet bracts, is a red plant
the last letter of JellicoE

explanation.surface: Admiral Jellicoe's large frame discovered in a Christmas flower display.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the poinsettia as one example of a red plant. The E goes between PLAN and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mars is one of the large bodies of the solar system, nicknamed for its rusty colour.

clue.text: Home-builder's hen producing good eggs?

parts.note: a brick is a good sort, a good egg
a layer is a hen that lays eggs

explanation.surface: A builder's chicken turning out top-quality eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'good egg' and a 'brick' are both old British praise for a reliable person, so a hen producing good eggs is a brick layer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bricklayer builds houses out of bricks.

clue.text: Lead removed from gold for instance, and the rest

indicators.note: the leading letter comes off the word

parts.note: gold is an example of a metal
the first letter of METAL, removed

explanation.surface: Separating lead from gold and other metals, as an alchemist might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the metal, which suits the gold nearby; it is the leading letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al, Latin et alii, means and the others.

clue.text: See 25
Inn's owner, sexy beast, seen by voyeur at first denied?

indicators.note: the first letter is refused

parts.note: hot = sexy
an elk is a large deer
PEEPER, a voyeur, without its first letter

explanation.surface: A randy innkeeper spied on by a peeping tom who then gets turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beast' is not a slur on the landlord but an animal: ELK.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotelkeeper owns or runs an inn or hotel.

clue.text: Dry northerly heading for Umbria, fast and swirling

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means reading upwards

parts.note: BRUT, dry of wine, read upwards

indicators.note: the first letter of Umbria

parts.note: first letter of Umbria
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: A weather report: a parched north wind sweeping fast and swirling over Umbria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry northerly' reads as a wind, but it is BRUT turned upwards; 'fast' is the noun, a period of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Turbulent air or water is swirling and disturbed.

clue.text: How a crocodile proceeds?

parts.note: read as the reptile, and meant as a British school outing walking in a line of pairs
how the line moves along, side by side in twos

explanation.surface: A question about how a reptile gets about.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a crocodile is a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs; the reptile also went into Noah's ark two by two.
explanation.definitionFit: A crocodile of pupils walks along in pairs, two by two.

clue.text: Kitty's up late — have really quick check?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read upwards

parts.note: POTS (kitty = pot, the pool of money) read upwards
the late X is the dead X

explanation.surface: A cat awake late at night, with a quick check of the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' is the pot of money, not the cat, and 'late' means deceased. 'check' is used in its sense of halt.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop dead is to check one's movement abruptly.

clue.text: See 1
Soldiers tense in ruin finding bomb

indicators.note: soldiers and tense go inside the word for ruin

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
OR = other ranks, ordinary soldiers
T = tense, the grammar abbreviation

explanation.surface: Nervous troops among ruins discovering an explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' is the grammatical term, not nervousness.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortar bomb is fired from a mortar; mortar is also short for the bomb.

clue.text: Red Sea to French crowd

parts.note: mer is French for sea
a lot = a group of people

explanation.surface: A trip across the Red Sea to a crowd of French people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Sea' splits: Red is the wine, and Sea turns French.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlot is a red wine grape and its wine.

clue.text: British send back spring rolls

indicators.note: the word for spring is turned round

parts.note: B = British
SPA, a mineral spring, turned round

explanation.surface: British diners returning spring rolls at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring rolls' is split: spring is the SPA and rolls the definition. A bap is a soft British bread roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Baps are soft round bread rolls.

clue.text: Are lives of camels and mules so onerous?

definitions.text: Are lives of camels and mules so onerous?

parts.note: pack animals, the classic beasts of burden
read as plain sympathy, and meant as a hint that their lives are full of the loads they carry

explanation.surface: A sympathetic question about the hard lot of pack animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as BURDEN + SOME, as in 'wholesome' or 'quarrelsome'; the lives of beasts of burden are full of burdens.
explanation.definitionFit: Burdensome means onerous, heavy to bear.

clue.text: Delay having suspect freed

indicators.note: the letters are doubtful, so not in their right order

parts.note: FREED rearranged

explanation.surface: A hold-up because a suspect has been released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' reads as the person released; it is an adjective telling you FREED is not to be trusted as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean postponing something to a later time.

clue.text: Certain as Pygmalion writer's sometimes said to be

indicators.note: in some accents the two words are said alike

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw wrote Pygmalion

explanation.surface: A remark that Shaw's own reputation for certainty is only sometimes justified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sometimes' is fair warning: SURE sounds like SHAW only in accents that say it 'shaw', common in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to be certain of something is to be quite sure of it.

clue.text: One booted and horsed, crossing over, would knee-length fit tight?

definitions.text: One booted and horsed, crossing over, would knee-length fit tight?

parts.note: read as any rider, and meant as the general whose name went on a boot and who rode Copenhagen at Waterloo
the answer crosses the grid, running from this across entry into 13 down
the knee-length rubber boot named after him ought to fit well, a hint at the second word

explanation.surface: An equestrian statue of a man in riding boots, and a question about whether tall boots fit snugly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing over' tells you the answer runs across into 13 down. The Wellington boot, knee-length and rubber, is named after the Duke.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo, is famous both for his boot and his horse Copenhagen.

clue.text: Young child, learner seen around a comprehensive

indicators.note: the letters are placed around the A

parts.note: a tot is a small child
as written
L = learner, from the L-plate

explanation.surface: A toddler and a learner watching around something.
explanation.walkthrough: TOT and L together sit around the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a total or comprehensive survey leaves nothing out.

clue.text: Piece in good works about divine persons

indicators.note: the Old Testament letters go round the persons

parts.note: OT = Old Testament, part of the Good Book
DD = Doctor of Divinity, a divine
men = people

explanation.surface: A religious article on the good deeds of holy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good works' is not charity but the Good Book's Old Testament; 'divine' is a noun, a clergyman with a divinity degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a stray leftover bit of cloth or stock is a piece, often sold as oddments.

clue.text: King wearing worthless items — that might do for Murphy

parts.note: R = rex, king
wearing a hat = in a hat
grot is British slang for junk

explanation.surface: A monarch dressed in rubbish, the sort of thing that would finish off an Irishman.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy is slang for a potato, and ring rot is a bacterial disease that ruins potato crops.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example using Irish slang: a murphy is a spud, and this bacterial blight kills potato crops.
